mekki-muskil:9-9.t: His saying, the Exalted: (قد أفلح من زكاها): in (زكى) there is a pronoun referring to (من), by which the ṣila (relative clause) is completed, i.e. "whoever purifies his soul by righteous deeds".

mekki-muskil:10-10.t: His saying (وقد خاب من دساها): i.e. he concealed his soul by evil deeds. It is also said that in (زكاها) and (دساها) there is a pronoun referring back to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, i.e. "whoever Allah purifies has succeeded, and whoever Allah forsakes has failed". This is far-fetched, since then no pronoun from its ṣila (relative clause) refers back to (من); the pronoun refers back only to the name of Allah, exalted be His mention. But if you make (من) a noun for the soul, and use the feminine according to the meaning, saying (زكاها) and (دساها), it is permissible, because the hāʾ and alif then refer back to (من), so the speech is sound; as if in the implied form it were "the soul which Allah purified has succeeded, and the soul which Allah forsook and concealed has failed"; and the meaning of (دساها) is "concealed it by evil deeds". Or (من) may mean the party, the faction or the group, so the hāʾ in (زكاها) and (دساها) refers back to (من), and the speech is good with the pronoun [of the verbs] in (زكاها) and (دساها) being for Allah, exalted be His mention. The origin of (دساها) is (دسسها), from "I hid (دسست) the thing" when you concealed it; but they replaced the last sīn with a yāʾ, and it turned into an alif because it was vowelled and what precedes it had fatḥa.

mekki-muskil:13-13.t: His saying (ناقة الله): accusative by way of incitement/warning (al-ighrāʾ), i.e. "beware of the she-camel of Allah". (وسقياها) is in the position of the accusative, conjoined to (ناقة).

mekki-muskil:14-14.t: His saying (فسواها): the hāʾ refers back to the destruction (الدمدمة), which His saying (فدمدم) indicates, i.e. He made them equal in the punishment.

mekki-muskil:15-15.t: His saying (فلا يخاف عقباها): whoever reads it with fāʾ, the verb belongs to Allah, exalted be His mention. Whoever reads it with wāw, the verb belongs to the one who hamstrung [the she-camel], i.e. "their most wretched one rose up and did not fear its consequence". It is also possible that whoever reads it with wāw makes the verb belong to Allah, as with the fāʾ.
